notes.front: What is the Mode C veil?
notes.back: Surface to 10,000 feet MSL within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, where an altitude-reporting (Mode C) transponder is required.
notes.explanation: Sectional charts outline it with a solid magenta line.
notes.example: Like a 30-mile circle drawn round a big-city airport, reaching well beyond the Class B shelves.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”
notes.evidence: Mode C Required Airspace (from the surface to 10,000' MSL) within a 30 NM radius of the primary airport(s) for which a

notes.front: What is special VFR (SVFR)?
notes.back: VFR flight with an ATC clearance under lower weather minimums, below 10,000 feet MSL within the surface area of controlled airspace around an airport.
notes.explanation: It is used instead of the basic VFR minimums of section 91.155.
notes.example: Like a special permit to use a road that is officially closed to ordinary traffic, granted one car at a time.
notes.evidence: special VFR operations may be conducted under the weather minimums and requirements of this section, instead of those contained in § 91.155, below 10,000 feet MSL

notes.front: What is a special flight rules area (SFRA)?
notes.back: Airspace of defined dimensions in which flight is subject to the special air traffic rules of part 93, unless ATC authorises otherwise.
notes.explanation: Each area has its own procedures, and SFRAs are shown on sectional and terminal area charts.
notes.example: Like a town centre with its own local traffic bylaws on top of the national rules.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-7, “Special Air Traffic Rules (SATR) and Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA)”
notes.evidence: Airspace of defined dimensions, above land areas or territorial waters, within which the flight of aircraft is subject to the rules set forth in 14 CFR part 93

notes.front: What is an air defense identification zone (ADIZ)?
notes.back: Airspace over land or water in which the ready identification, location and control of all aircraft is required for national security.
notes.explanation: Defense and law enforcement aircraft are excepted from the requirement.
notes.example: Like a border checkpoint in the sky, where every aircraft must be identifiable before it crosses.
notes.evidence: means an area of airspace over land or water, in which the ready identification, location, and control of all aircraft (except Department of Defense and law enforcement aircraft) is required in the interest of national security

notes.front: What is a Federal airway?
notes.back: A Class E airspace area that, unless otherwise specified, extends from 1,200 feet AGL up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: Federal airways are part of the Class E airspace used for en route flight.
notes.example: Like a charted motorway in the sky, marked on the chart and made of controlled airspace.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-6, “Class E Airspace”
notes.evidence: Federal airways and low-altitude RNAV routes are Class E airspace areas and, unless otherwise specified, extend upward from 1,200 feet AGL to, but not including,18,000 feet MSL.

notes.front: What is a VFR cruising altitude?
notes.back: The altitude that section 91.159 requires in level VFR cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface, chosen by magnetic course.
notes.explanation: The rule sets odd or even thousands plus 500 feet depending on the direction of flight.
notes.example: Like driving on the correct side of the road, but choosing a height band by direction.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: each person operating an aircraft under VFR in level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface shall maintain the appropriate altitude or flight level prescribed below

notes.front: What are the VFR visibility and cloud clearance minimums in Class B airspace?
notes.back: 3 statute miles, and clear of clouds.
notes.explanation: Unlike Classes C and D, Class B sets no distance from cloud.
notes.evidence: Class B 3 statute miles Clear of Clouds.

notes.front: What are the VFR visibility and cloud clearance minimums in Class C airspace?
notes.back: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: Classes C and D, and E below 10,000 feet MSL, share these minimums.
notes.evidence: Class C 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.

notes.front: What are the VFR visibility and cloud clearance minimums in Class D airspace?
notes.back: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: They are the same as in Class C.
notes.evidence: Class D 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.

notes.front: What are the VFR minimums in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL?
notes.back: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: At or above 10,000 feet MSL the Class E minimums increase.
notes.evidence: Less than 10,000 feet MSL 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.

notes.front: What are the VFR minimums in Class E airspace at or above 10,000 feet MSL?
notes.back: 5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: The same line applies in Class G more than 1,200 feet above the surface and at or above 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.evidence: At or above 10,000 feet MSL 5 statute miles 1,000 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 1 statute mile horizontal.

notes.front: In Class G airspace at 1,200 feet or less above the surface, by day, what are the VFR minimums for an aeroplane?
notes.back: 1 statute mile, and clear of clouds.
notes.explanation: This applies whatever the MSL altitude, as long as you are within 1,200 feet of the surface.
notes.evidence: Day, except as provided in § 91.155(b) 1 statute mile Clear of clouds.

notes.front: In Class G airspace at 1,200 feet or less above the surface, at night, what are the VFR minimums for an aeroplane?
notes.back: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: An exception allows 1 mile clear of clouds in the traffic pattern within half a mile of the runway.
notes.evidence: Night, except as provided in § 91.155(b) 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.

notes.front: In Class G more than 1,200 feet above the surface but below 10,000 feet MSL, what are the VFR minimums by day?
notes.back: 1 statute mile; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: Visibility stays at 1 mile, but you must now keep a set distance from cloud.
notes.evidence: More than 1,200 feet above the surface but less than 10,000 feet MSL Day 1 statute mile 500 feet below.

notes.front: In Class G more than 1,200 feet above the surface but below 10,000 feet MSL, what are the VFR minimums at night?
notes.back: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: The night visibility requirement is three times the day figure.
notes.evidence: Night 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal. More than 1,200 feet above the surface and at or above 10,000 feet MSL

notes.front: In Class G more than 1,200 feet above the surface and at or above 10,000 feet MSL, what are the VFR minimums?
notes.back: 5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontally from clouds.
notes.explanation: They match Class E at or above 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.evidence: More than 1,200 feet above the surface and at or above 10,000 feet MSL 5 statute miles 1,000 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 1 statute mile horizontal.

notes.front: What VFR weather minimums does section 91.155 give for Class A airspace?
notes.back: None: “Not Applicable”.
notes.explanation: All flight in Class A is under IFR, so VFR minimums have no meaning there.
notes.evidence: Class A Not Applicable Not Applicable.

notes.front: In controlled airspace that reaches the surface around an airport, what is the lowest ceiling beneath which you may fly under basic VFR?
notes.back: 1,000 feet (unless under special VFR).
notes.explanation: The rule applies within the lateral boundaries of the controlled airspace designated to the surface.
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft beneath the ceiling under VFR within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport when the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet

notes.front: What ground visibility is needed to take off, land or enter the traffic pattern under VFR within the surface area of Class B, C, D or E airspace?
notes.back: At least 3 statute miles (flight visibility of 3 miles if ground visibility is not reported).
notes.explanation: Special VFR is the exception written into the rule.
notes.evidence: Unless ground visibility at that airport is at least 3 statute miles

notes.front: Cleared through Class B, you are passing 300 feet below a cloud layer with 4 statute miles visibility. Are you meeting the VFR minimums?
notes.back: A) Yes: Class B needs 3 statute miles and clear of clouds
notes.choices:
A) Yes: Class B needs 3 statute miles and clear of clouds
B) No: you must stay 500 feet below the cloud
C) No: Class B needs 5 statute miles
notes.choicesExplained: B gives the Class C, D and low Class E cloud distance. C gives the minimum for 10,000 feet MSL and above.
notes.explanation: In Class B you need only stay clear of clouds with 3 statute miles visibility.
notes.evidence: Class B 3 statute miles Clear of Clouds.

notes.front: In Class C airspace you are flying 700 feet above the tops of a scattered cloud layer with 6 miles visibility. Are you legal under VFR?
notes.back: B) No: you must be at least 1,000 feet above cloud
notes.choices:
A) Yes, since you are clear of the cloud
B) No: you must be at least 1,000 feet above cloud
C) No: you must be 2,000 feet above cloud
notes.choicesExplained: A is the Class B rule, not Class C. C: 2,000 feet is the horizontal distance, not the vertical one above.
notes.explanation: Class C requires 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally.
notes.evidence: Class C 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.

notes.front: You are cruising VFR at 10,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace with 4 statute miles flight visibility. Are you legal?
notes.back: B) No: at or above 10,000 feet MSL you need 5 statute miles
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 3 statute miles is enough in Class E
B) No: at or above 10,000 feet MSL you need 5 statute miles
C) Yes, if you stay clear of clouds
notes.choicesExplained: A applies only below 10,000 feet MSL. C: clear of clouds is the Class B rule.
notes.explanation: The Class E minimums rise at 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.evidence: At or above 10,000 feet MSL 5 statute miles 1,000 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 1 statute mile horizontal.

notes.front: By day in Class G, 900 feet above the ground, you have 1.5 statute miles visibility and are clear of clouds. Are you meeting the VFR minimums?
notes.back: A) Yes: 1 statute mile and clear of clouds is enough
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 1 statute mile and clear of clouds is enough
B) No: you need 3 statute miles
C) No: you must stay 500 feet below cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B is the night minimum. C applies above 1,200 feet above the surface.
notes.explanation: Low Class G by day needs only 1 statute mile and clear of clouds.
notes.evidence: Day, except as provided in § 91.155(b) 1 statute mile Clear of clouds.

notes.front: At night in Class G, 1,000 feet above the ground and 10 miles from any airport, you have 2 statute miles visibility. Can you continue VFR?
notes.back: B) No: at night you need 3 statute miles, unless in the pattern within half a mile of the runway
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 1 statute mile is enough in Class G
B) No: at night you need 3 statute miles, unless in the pattern within half a mile of the runway
C) Yes, because you are below 1,200 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A and C use the day minimum; at night the low Class G minimum is 3 statute miles.
notes.explanation: You are nowhere near a traffic pattern, so the pattern exception does not help.
notes.evidence: Night, except as provided in § 91.155(b) 3 statute miles 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.

notes.front: By day in Class G, 2,500 feet above the ground and well below 10,000 feet MSL, you have 3 statute miles visibility and are 300 feet below cloud. Are you legal?
notes.back: B) No: you must be at least 500 feet below the cloud
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 1 statute mile and clear of clouds
B) No: you must be at least 500 feet below the cloud
C) Yes, because visibility is above 1 statute mile
notes.choicesExplained: A and C use the low Class G rule, which applies only at or below 1,200 feet above the surface.
notes.explanation: Above 1,200 feet above the surface, Class G by day needs 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal.
notes.evidence: More than 1,200 feet above the surface but less than 10,000 feet MSL Day 1 statute mile 500 feet below.

notes.front: Your home airport has a Class E surface area, and the ceiling is reported at 800 feet with 5 miles visibility. Can you depart under basic VFR beneath the ceiling?
notes.back: B) No, not under basic VFR; you could ask ATC for special VFR
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if you stay clear of clouds
B) No, not under basic VFR; you could ask ATC for special VFR
C) Yes, because Class E has no ceiling rule
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the 1,000-foot ceiling rule for surface areas. C: the rule covers any controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport.
notes.explanation: The ceiling rule has an exception only for special VFR.
notes.evidence: Except as provided in § 91.157, no person may operate an aircraft beneath the ceiling under VFR within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport

notes.front: A Class D airport reports ground visibility of 2 statute miles and a ceiling of 3,000 feet. Can you land there under basic VFR?
notes.back: B) No: you need at least 3 statute miles ground visibility, or a special VFR clearance
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 2 miles is enough in Class D
B) No: you need at least 3 statute miles ground visibility, or a special VFR clearance
C) Yes, if flight visibility in the air is better
notes.choicesExplained: A is below the 3-mile ground visibility minimum. C: flight visibility counts only if ground visibility is not reported.
notes.explanation: Reported ground visibility governs taking off, landing and entering the pattern.
notes.evidence: If ground visibility is not reported at that airport, unless flight visibility during landing or takeoff, or while operating in the traffic pattern is at least 3 statute miles

notes.front: How do the VFR cloud clearance minimums of Class B differ from those of Class C?
notes.back: Class B: clear of clouds. Class C: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal. Both need 3 statute miles.
notes.explanation: Both classes need 3 statute miles of visibility; only the cloud clearance differs.
notes.evidence: Class B 3 statute miles Clear of Clouds. Class C 3 statute miles 500 feet below.

notes.front: Where may special VFR be flown?
notes.back: Below 10,000 feet MSL, within the upward extension of the surface area of controlled airspace for an airport.
notes.explanation: It is available only inside that surface-area airspace, not elsewhere.
notes.evidence: below 10,000 feet MSL within the airspace contained by the upward extension of the lateral boundaries of the controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport

notes.front: What must you have from ATC before flying special VFR?
notes.back: An ATC clearance.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the conditions section 91.157 lists.
notes.evidence: Special VFR operations may only be conducted— (1) With an ATC clearance;

notes.front: Under special VFR, what cloud clearance is required?
notes.back: Clear of clouds.
notes.explanation: No set distance from cloud applies, unlike basic VFR in a surface area.
notes.evidence: With an ATC clearance; (2) Clear of clouds;

notes.front: Under special VFR, what flight visibility does an aeroplane need?
notes.back: At least 1 statute mile.
notes.explanation: Helicopters are excepted from this visibility figure.
notes.evidence: Except for helicopters, when flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile

notes.front: To take off or land an aeroplane under special VFR, what ground visibility is needed?
notes.back: At least 1 statute mile (flight visibility of 1 mile if ground visibility is not reported).
notes.explanation: Again, helicopters are excepted.
notes.evidence: No person may take off or land an aircraft (other than a helicopter) under special VFR— (1) Unless ground visibility is at least 1 statute mile

notes.front: What does an aeroplane pilot need to fly special VFR between sunset and sunrise?
notes.back: To meet the part 61 requirements for instrument flight, in an aircraft equipped as section 91.205(d) requires.
notes.explanation: Otherwise, special VFR in an aeroplane is limited to between sunrise and sunset.
notes.evidence: The person being granted the ATC clearance meets the applicable requirements for instrument flight under part 61 of this chapter; and (ii) The aircraft is equipped as required in § 91.205(d).

notes.front: A private pilot with no instrument rating wants a special VFR clearance to depart after sunset in poor visibility. Can they take it?
notes.back: B) No: at night special VFR needs instrument qualification and an instrument-equipped aircraft
notes.choices:
A) Yes, with a clearance and 1 mile visibility
B) No: at night special VFR needs instrument qualification and an instrument-equipped aircraft
C) Yes, if the ceiling is above 1,000 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A gives the daytime conditions only. C: no ceiling removes the sunrise-to-sunset limit on special VFR in an aeroplane.
notes.explanation: For aeroplanes, special VFR is otherwise limited to between sunrise and sunset.
notes.evidence: between sunrise and sunset (or in Alaska, when the sun is 6 degrees or less below the horizon) unless

notes.front: By day, a Class D airport reports 1.5 statute miles visibility and a ceiling of 600 feet. You can stay clear of clouds. Can you depart under special VFR?
notes.back: A) Yes: 1.5 miles, clear of clouds, with a clearance
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 1.5 miles, clear of clouds, with a clearance
B) No: special VFR needs 3 statute miles
C) No: special VFR is never allowed in Class D
notes.choicesExplained: B is the basic VFR figure. C: special VFR is for the surface areas of controlled airspace, such as Class D.
notes.explanation: By day an aeroplane needs a clearance, clear of clouds and 1 statute mile.
notes.evidence: Except for helicopters, when flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile

notes.front: Under what flight rules must you operate in Class A airspace?
notes.back: IFR, unless otherwise authorised.
notes.explanation: Class A generally runs from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-2, “Class A Airspace”
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise authorized, all persons must operate their aircraft under IFR.

notes.front: A VFR pilot plans to climb to 19,000 feet MSL to find a tailwind. Can the flight stay VFR?
notes.back: B) No: Class A starts at 18,000 feet MSL and requires IFR
notes.choices:
A) Yes, with 5 statute miles visibility
B) No: Class A starts at 18,000 feet MSL and requires IFR
C) Yes, above 18,000 feet only with oxygen
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the high-altitude VFR minimums, which do not exist in Class A. C: oxygen does not change the flight rules.
notes.explanation: VFR weather minimums are “not applicable” in Class A.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-2, “Class A Airspace”
notes.evidence: Generally, that airspace from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600

notes.front: What must you receive before operating in Class B airspace?
notes.back: An ATC clearance from the facility with jurisdiction, regardless of weather.
notes.explanation: All cleared aircraft in Class B receive separation services.
notes.evidence: The operator must receive an ATC clearance from the ATC facility having jurisdiction for that area before operating an aircraft in that area.

notes.front: To operate in Class B airspace, what certificate must the pilot in command generally hold?
notes.back: At least a private pilot certificate, unless a student, sport or recreational pilot has met the specific training requirements.
notes.explanation: A student pilot may fly solo there only after meeting section 61.94 or 61.95.
notes.evidence: The pilot in command holds at least a private pilot certificate

notes.front: Before solo flight in a Class B area, what endorsement does a student pilot need?
notes.back: A logbook endorsement from the instructor who trained them there, dated within the preceding 90 days, for that specific Class B area.
notes.explanation: The student must also have had ground and flight training on that Class B area.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.95, “Operations in Class B airspace and at airports located within Class B airspace”
notes.evidence: the endorsement is dated within the 90-day period preceding the date of the flight in that Class B airspace area

notes.front: For all operations in Class B airspace, what radio must the aircraft carry?
notes.back: An operable two-way radio able to talk to ATC on the Class B frequencies.
notes.explanation: Navigation equipment is added only for IFR operation.
notes.evidence: For all operations. An operable two-way radio capable of communications with ATC on appropriate frequencies for that Class B airspace area.

notes.front: Besides a radio, what altitude-reporting equipment must an aircraft have in Class B airspace?
notes.back: An operating transponder with automatic altitude reporting.
notes.explanation: The details are in section 91.215(a).
notes.evidence: The applicable operating transponder and automatic altitude reporting equipment specified in § 91.215

notes.front: Since 1 January 2020, what broadcast surveillance equipment must an aircraft have in Class B airspace?
notes.back: ADS-B Out equipment meeting section 91.225.
notes.explanation: It is required alongside the transponder, not instead of it.
notes.evidence: After January 1, 2020, the applicable Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast Out equipment specified in § 91.225.

notes.front: Approaching Class B, you have called approach and they have replied with your call sign and a squawk code, but have not said “cleared into the Class B”. What do you do?
notes.back: B) Stay outside Class B until you hear an explicit clearance
notes.choices:
A) Enter: two-way radio contact is enough
B) Stay outside Class B until you hear an explicit clearance
C) Enter if the weather is good VFR
notes.choicesExplained: A is the Class C and D rule, not Class B. C: a clearance is needed regardless of the weather.
notes.explanation: Class B entry needs an ATC clearance, not just two-way contact.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-3, “Class B Airspace”
notes.evidence: Regardless of weather conditions, an ATC clearance is required prior to operating within Class B airspace.

notes.front: A student pilot wants to fly solo into a Class B area they have never trained in. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B) No: they need the ground and flight training for that Class B area and a current endorsement
notes.choices:
A) Yes: a student certificate is enough
B) No: they need the ground and flight training for that Class B area and a current endorsement
C) No: students may never fly in Class B
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores section 61.95. C: students may fly solo there once they meet section 61.95.
notes.explanation: The endorsement must be for that specific Class B area and dated within 90 days.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.95, “Operations in Class B airspace and at airports located within Class B airspace”
notes.evidence: The student pilot has received both ground and flight training from an authorized instructor on that Class B airspace area

notes.front: An aeroplane has a working two-way radio and a Mode C transponder but no ADS-B Out. Can it be flown into Class B today?
notes.back: B) No: Class B also needs ADS-B Out, unless ATC authorises otherwise
notes.choices:
A) Yes: radio and transponder are enough
B) No: Class B also needs ADS-B Out, unless ATC authorises otherwise
C) Yes, if the pilot holds a private pilot certificate
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out the ADS-B Out requirement in force since 1 January 2020. C: the pilot certificate does not replace equipment.
notes.explanation: Class B needs all three: two-way radio, altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out.
notes.evidence: After January 1, 2020, the applicable Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast Out equipment specified in § 91.225.

notes.front: What must you do before entering Class C airspace?
notes.back: Establish two-way radio communications with the ATC facility providing air traffic services, and keep them while inside.
notes.explanation: A clearance is not required, unlike Class B.
notes.evidence: Each person must establish two-way radio communications with the ATC facility (including foreign ATC in the case of foreign airspace designated in the United States) providing air traffic services prior to entering that airspace

notes.front: What are the usual dimensions of the Class C core surface area?
notes.back: A 5 NM radius from the surface up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation.
notes.explanation: The height is charted in MSL.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: the airspace usually consists of a 5 NM radius core surface area that extends from the surface up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation

notes.front: What are the usual dimensions of the Class C shelf area?
notes.back: A 10 NM radius, from no lower than 1,200 feet up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation.
notes.explanation: Each Class C area is individually tailored, so the chart is the final word.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: a 10 NM radius shelf area that extends no lower than 1,200 feet up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation

notes.front: What equipment does Class C airspace require?
notes.back: A two-way radio, a transponder with altitude reporting, and ADS-B Out (unless ATC authorises otherwise).
notes.explanation: No specific pilot certificate is required.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, an operable radar beacon transponder with automatic altitude reporting capability and operable ADS-B Out equipment.

notes.front: You are flying 8 NM from a Class C primary airport at 900 feet above the airport elevation. Using the usual dimensions, are you inside Class C?
notes.back: B) No: the shelf starts no lower than 1,200 feet above the airport, so you are beneath it
notes.choices:
A) Yes: you are inside the shelf area
B) No: the shelf starts no lower than 1,200 feet above the airport, so you are beneath it
C) Yes: Class C starts at the surface everywhere within 10 NM
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the shelf floor. C: only the 5 NM core reaches the surface.
notes.explanation: Between 5 and 10 NM, Class C usually begins at 1,200 feet above the airport.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: a 10 NM radius shelf area that extends no lower than 1,200 feet up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation

notes.front: You call Class C or D and the controller answers “[your call sign], standby”. Have two-way communications been established?
notes.back: Yes: you may enter.
notes.explanation: The controller used your call sign, which is what counts.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: If the controller responds to a radio call with, “(aircraft callsign) standby,” radio communications have been established and the pilot can enter the Class C airspace.

notes.front: The controller replies to your initial call without using your call sign. Have communications been established?
notes.back: No: you may not enter the Class C or D airspace.
notes.explanation: Only a reply that uses your aircraft identification establishes communications.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: if the controller responds to the initial radio call without using the aircraft identification, radio communications have not been established and the pilot may not enter the Class C airspace

notes.front: Which reply lets you enter Class C airspace?
notes.back: B) “Cessna 4321X, standby.”
notes.choices:
A) “Aircraft calling Riverside Approach, standby.”
B) “Cessna 4321X, standby.”
C) “Station calling, say again.”
notes.choicesExplained: A and C do not use your call sign, so communications have not been established.
notes.explanation: Hearing your own call sign is the test; “standby” does not stop you entering.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-4, “Class C Airspace”
notes.evidence: If the controller responds to a radio call with, “(aircraft callsign) standby,” radio communications have been established

notes.front: What must you do before entering Class D airspace?
notes.back: Establish two-way radio communications with the ATC facility providing air traffic services, and keep them while inside.
notes.explanation: The Class D rule is written the same way as the Class C one.
notes.evidence: Each person must establish two-way radio communications with the ATC facility (including foreign ATC in the case of foreign airspace designated in the United States) providing air traffic services prior to entering that airspace

notes.front: Generally, how high does Class D airspace extend?
notes.back: From the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation (charted in MSL).
notes.explanation: It surrounds airports that have an operational control tower.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-5, “Class D Airspace”
notes.evidence: Generally, Class D airspace extends upward from the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation (charted in MSL)

notes.front: Approaching a Class D airport, you call the tower and hear “Cessna 52Y, remain clear, standby.” What should you do?
notes.back: A) Stay outside until the controller says conditions permit entry
notes.choices:
A) Stay outside until the controller says conditions permit entry
B) Enter: your call sign was used, so communications are established
C) Enter, but keep clear of the traffic pattern
notes.choicesExplained: B: communications are established, but the controller has told you to remain outside. C: the instruction is to stay outside the airspace altogether.
notes.explanation: If traffic prevents entry, the controller tells the pilot to remain outside until conditions permit.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-5, “Class D Airspace”
notes.evidence: If workload or traffic conditions prevent immediate entry into Class D airspace, the controller will inform the pilot to remain outside the Class D airspace until conditions permit entry.

notes.front: How does the entry requirement for Class B differ from that for Classes C and D?
notes.back: Class B needs an ATC clearance; Classes C and D need two-way radio communications established before entry.
notes.explanation: Hearing your call sign is enough for C or D, but not for B.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-3, “Class B Airspace”
notes.evidence: Regardless of weather conditions, an ATC clearance is required prior to operating within Class B airspace.

notes.front: Which Class E airspace begins at the surface around an airport?
notes.back: A Class E surface area, designated for an airport where a control tower is not in operation.
notes.explanation: The airport must have weather reporting and communications down to the runway surface.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-6, “Class E Airspace”
notes.evidence: Surface area designated for an airport where a control tower is not in operation.

notes.front: On a sectional chart, what does a magenta vignette show about Class E?
notes.back: A transition area where Class E begins at 700 feet AGL.
notes.explanation: Such areas serve airports with an approved instrument procedure.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-6, “Class E Airspace”
notes.evidence: Class E transition areas extend upward from either 700 feet AGL (shown as magenta vignette on sectional charts)

notes.front: On a sectional chart, what does a blue vignette show about Class E?
notes.back: A transition area where Class E begins at 1,200 feet AGL.
notes.explanation: The 700-foot and 1,200-foot transition areas stay in effect all the time.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-6, “Class E Airspace”
notes.evidence: or 1,200 feet AGL (blue vignette) and are designated for airports with an approved instrument procedure

notes.front: Where no lower floor is designated, from what altitude does Class E begin over the 48 contiguous states?
notes.back: 14,500 feet MSL, up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: Airspace below 1,500 feet above the surface is excluded from this layer.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-6, “Class E Airspace”
notes.evidence: The airspace extending upward from 14,500 feet MSL to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL overlying the 48 contiguous states

notes.front: You are 1,000 feet above the ground inside a magenta vignette, away from any surface area. What class of airspace are you in?
notes.back: A) Class E
notes.choices:
A) Class E
B) Class G
notes.choicesExplained: B: below 700 feet AGL here you would be in Class G, but at 1,000 feet you are above the Class E floor.
notes.explanation: A magenta vignette marks Class E starting at 700 feet AGL.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-2-6, “Class E Airspace”
notes.evidence: Class E transition areas extend upward from either 700 feet AGL (shown as magenta vignette on sectional charts)

notes.front: You are 1,000 feet above the ground in open country, outside any vignette or airway, where the chart shows Class E beginning at 1,200 feet AGL. What class are you in?
notes.back: B) Class G
notes.choices:
A) Class E
B) Class G
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class E here starts at 1,200 feet AGL, above you.
notes.explanation: Class G is whatever airspace has not been designated Class A to E.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-3-1, “Class G Airspace: General”
notes.evidence: Class G airspace (uncontrolled) is that portion of airspace that has not been designated as Class A, Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E airspace.

notes.front: What is Class G airspace?
notes.back: Uncontrolled airspace: whatever has not been designated Class A, B, C, D or E.
notes.explanation: VFR flight there still follows the visibility and cloud minimums of section 91.155.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-3-1, “Class G Airspace: General”
notes.evidence: Class G airspace (uncontrolled) is that portion of airspace that has not been designated as Class A, Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E airspace.

notes.front: Below 10,000 feet MSL, what is the maximum indicated airspeed, unless the Administrator authorises otherwise?
notes.back: 250 knots.
notes.explanation: If a type’s minimum safe airspeed is higher than a limit, it may fly at that minimum.
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots

notes.front: Within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport, at or below 2,500 feet above the surface, what is the speed limit?
notes.back: 200 knots indicated, unless ATC authorises or requires otherwise.
notes.explanation: This paragraph does not apply inside Class B, where the 250-knot rule applies.
notes.evidence: at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots

notes.front: In the airspace underlying Class B, or in a VFR corridor through it, what is the speed limit?
notes.back: 200 knots indicated.
notes.explanation: The same limit covers both the airspace beneath and the corridors through Class B.
notes.evidence: in the airspace underlying a Class B airspace area designated for an airport or in a VFR corridor designated through such a Class B airspace area, at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots

notes.front: You are 3 NM from a Class D primary airport at 1,500 feet above the surface. What is your maximum indicated airspeed?
notes.back: B) 200 knots
notes.choices:
A) 250 knots
B) 200 knots
C) No limit applies below Class D
notes.choicesExplained: A is the general limit below 10,000 feet MSL, but the Class D rule is lower. C: the rule covers all airspace at or below 2,500 feet within 4 NM.
notes.explanation: Inside 4 NM and at or below 2,500 feet, the 200-knot limit applies.
notes.evidence: at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area

notes.front: Anywhere, what minimum altitude does section 91.119 require (except for take-off and landing)?
notes.back: One that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property if a power unit fails.
notes.explanation: This applies on top of the specific figures for congested and other areas.
notes.evidence: An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface.

notes.front: Over a congested area or an open-air assembly of people, what is the minimum altitude?
notes.back: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet.
notes.explanation: The same rule covers cities, towns, settlements and open-air crowds.
notes.evidence: an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft

notes.front: Over other than congested areas, what is the minimum altitude?
notes.back: 500 feet above the surface.
notes.explanation: Over open water or sparsely populated areas, a distance rule applies instead.
notes.evidence: Over other than congested areas. An altitude of 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas.

notes.front: Over open water or sparsely populated areas, how close may you fly to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure?
notes.back: No closer than 500 feet.
notes.explanation: It replaces the 500-feet-above-the-surface rule in these areas.
notes.evidence: the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure

notes.front: Over a town, the tallest obstacle within 2,000 feet of you is a 300-foot radio mast. What is your minimum altitude above the ground?
notes.back: B) 1,300 feet above the ground
notes.choices:
A) 1,000 feet above the ground
B) 1,300 feet above the ground
C) 500 feet above the mast
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the mast. C: the 500-foot rule for other than congested areas is measured from the surface, and it does not apply over a town.
notes.explanation: You need 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally.
notes.evidence: an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft

notes.front: Over empty farmland you pass 600 feet from a lone barn, at 400 feet above the ground. Are you legal under section 91.119?
notes.back: A) Yes: over sparse areas you need only 500 feet from any person or structure
notes.choices:
A) Yes: over sparse areas you need only 500 feet from any person or structure
B) No: you must be 1,000 feet above the barn
C) No: you must be 500 feet above the ground everywhere
notes.choicesExplained: B is the congested-area rule. C: over sparsely populated areas the 500-foot distance rule replaces the height rule.
notes.explanation: You must also still be able to make an emergency landing without undue hazard.
notes.evidence: the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure

notes.front: Below 18,000 feet MSL, on a magnetic course of 0° to 179°, what VFR cruising altitudes apply?
notes.back: Odd thousands of feet MSL plus 500 (3,500, 5,500, 7,500 and so on).
notes.explanation: It applies only in level cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of zero degrees through 179 degrees, any odd thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet (such as 3,500, 5,500, or 7,500)

notes.front: Below 18,000 feet MSL, on a magnetic course of 180° to 359°, what VFR cruising altitudes apply?
notes.back: Even thousands of feet MSL plus 500 (4,500, 6,500, 8,500 and so on).
notes.explanation: It applies only in level cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of 180 degrees through 359 degrees, any even thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet (such as 4,500, 6,500, or 8,500)

notes.front: Above what height over the surface do the VFR cruising altitude rules apply?
notes.back: More than 3,000 feet above the surface, in level cruising flight.
notes.explanation: Holding patterns of 2 minutes or less, and turns, are excepted.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: in level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface

notes.front: Your magnetic course is 095° and the terrain is at 1,000 feet MSL. Which of these is a correct VFR cruising altitude?
notes.back: B) 5,500 feet MSL
notes.choices:
A) 4,500 feet MSL
B) 5,500 feet MSL
C) 6,000 feet MSL
notes.choicesExplained: A is for westbound courses. C is not a thousand plus 500.
notes.explanation: On courses of 0° to 179° magnetic, cruise at odd thousands plus 500.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of zero degrees through 179 degrees, any odd thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet

notes.front: Your magnetic course is 250° and you are well over 3,000 feet above the ground. Which is a correct VFR cruising altitude?
notes.back: B) 8,500 feet MSL
notes.choices:
A) 7,500 feet MSL
B) 8,500 feet MSL
C) 8,000 feet MSL
notes.choicesExplained: A is for eastbound courses. C is not a thousand plus 500.
notes.explanation: On courses of 180° to 359° magnetic, cruise at even thousands plus 500.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of 180 degrees through 359 degrees, any even thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet

notes.front: You plan to cruise at 2,500 feet above the ground on a course of 045° magnetic. Does the VFR cruising altitude rule dictate your altitude?
notes.back: B) No: the rule applies only more than 3,000 feet above the surface
notes.choices:
A) Yes: you must use 3,500 feet
B) No: the rule applies only more than 3,000 feet above the surface
C) Yes: every VFR cruise needs a thousand plus 500
notes.choicesExplained: A and C forget the 3,000-foot threshold.
notes.explanation: Below that height, the other rules, such as minimum safe altitudes, still apply.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: in level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface

notes.front: For VFR cruising altitudes, is the direction based on magnetic course, true course or heading?
notes.back: Magnetic course.
notes.explanation: Section 91.159 states both direction bands as magnetic courses.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.159, “VFR cruising altitude or flight level”
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of zero degrees through 179 degrees

notes.front: Within 30 NM of a listed Class B primary airport, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, what equipment is required?
notes.back: A transponder with automatic pressure altitude reporting (Mode C), and ADS-B Out.
notes.explanation: This is the Mode C veil: section 91.215 requires the transponder, and section 91.225(d)(2) adds ADS-B Out over the same area. Some aircraft without an engine-driven electrical system are excepted.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: In all airspace within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in appendix D, section 1 of this part from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL

notes.front: In which classes of airspace do all aircraft need a transponder with altitude reporting?
notes.back: Class A, Class B and Class C.
notes.explanation: Other areas, such as the Mode C veil and above 10,000 feet MSL, are added by section 91.215 too.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: All aircraft. In Class A, Class B, and Class C airspace areas;

notes.front: Above the ceiling of a Class B or Class C area, within its lateral boundaries, up to what altitude is a transponder required?
notes.back: 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: The requirement follows the lateral limits of the area upward.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: All aircraft in all airspace above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of a Class B or Class C airspace area designated for an airport upward to 10,000 feet MSL

notes.front: Over the 48 contiguous states, at and above 10,000 feet MSL, where is a transponder not required?
notes.back: In the airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface.
notes.explanation: Aircraft not certificated with an engine-driven electrical system, balloons and gliders are also excepted.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: In all airspace of the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface

notes.front: When must an equipped aircraft operate its transponder, including Mode C?
notes.back: In the airspace listed in section 91.215(b) and in all controlled airspace.
notes.explanation: It must reply on the appropriate code or the one ATC assigns.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: while in the airspace as specified in paragraph (b) of this section or in all controlled airspace, each person operating an aircraft equipped with an operable ATC transponder

notes.front: Since 1 January 2020, in which airspace is ADS-B Out required below 18,000 feet MSL?
notes.back: Class B and C, the Mode C veil, above Class B and C up to 10,000 feet, and Class E at and above 10,000 feet.
notes.explanation: The Class E part excludes airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface. Section 91.225 also covers Class E from 3,000 feet MSL over the Gulf of Mexico, within 12 NM of the coast.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.225, “Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use”
notes.evidence: Class B and Class C airspace areas;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Your aircraft has an electrical system but its transponder has been removed. You plan to fly 20 NM from a Class B primary airport, under the shelves at 2,000 feet. Can you go?
notes.back: B) No: within the 30 NM veil you need Mode C and ADS-B Out, unless ATC authorises otherwise
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if you stay below the Class B shelves
B) No: within the 30 NM veil you need Mode C and ADS-B Out, unless ATC authorises otherwise
C) Yes, below 2,500 feet above the ground
notes.choicesExplained: A: the veil runs from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, not just inside Class B. C: the 2,500-foot exclusion is for the rule at and above 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: For an aircraft with no transponder, a deviation must be requested at least an hour ahead.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: In all airspace within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in appendix D, section 1 of this part from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL

notes.front: You plan to overfly a Class C area at 6,500 feet MSL, above its ceiling, within its lateral limits. Do you need a Mode C transponder?
notes.back: B) Yes: a transponder with altitude reporting is required above Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL
notes.choices:
A) No: you are above the Class C, so no equipment rule applies
B) Yes: a transponder with altitude reporting is required above Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL
C) Only if you talk to approach
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores section 91.215(b)(4). C: the rule applies whether or not you talk to anyone.
notes.explanation: The requirement extends above the ceiling within the lateral boundaries.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.215, “ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use”
notes.evidence: All aircraft in all airspace above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of a Class B or Class C airspace area designated for an airport upward to 10,000 feet MSL

notes.front: What is prohibited within a prohibited area?
notes.back: The flight of aircraft.
notes.explanation: They are set up for security or other reasons of national welfare and are shown on charts.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-4-2, “Prohibited Areas”
notes.evidence: identified by an area on the surface of the earth within which the flight of aircraft is prohibited

notes.front: What kind of hazards do restricted areas denote?
notes.back: Unusual, often invisible hazards to aircraft, such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery or guided missiles.
notes.explanation: Flight there is not wholly prohibited but is subject to restrictions.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-4-3, “Restricted Areas”
notes.evidence: Restricted areas denote the existence of unusual, often invisible, hazards to aircraft such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery, or guided missiles.

notes.front: What does the Aeronautical Information Manual say about entering a restricted area without authorisation from the using or controlling agency?
notes.back: It may be extremely hazardous to the aircraft and its occupants.
notes.explanation: Restricted areas are published in the Federal Register as regulatory airspace.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-4-3, “Restricted Areas”
notes.evidence: Penetration of restricted areas without authorization from the using or controlling agency may be extremely hazardous to the aircraft and its occupants.

notes.front: Your direct route crosses a restricted area that is active today. What should you do?
notes.back: B) Get authorisation from the using or controlling agency, or route around it
notes.choices:
A) Fly through: VFR aircraft may cross restricted areas freely
B) Get authorisation from the using or controlling agency, or route around it
C) Fly through above 5,000 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A: flight is subject to restrictions and can be extremely hazardous. C: an altitude alone gives no authorisation.
notes.explanation: The hazards inside, such as gunnery, are often invisible.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-4-3, “Restricted Areas”
notes.evidence: Penetration of restricted areas without authorization from the using or controlling agency may be extremely hazardous

notes.front: May VFR pilots fly through an active MOA, and with what caution?
notes.back: Yes, but with extreme caution while military activity is going on.
notes.explanation: Before entering an active MOA, contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-4-5, “Military Operations Areas”
notes.evidence: Pilots operating under VFR should exercise extreme caution while flying within a MOA when military activity is being conducted.

notes.front: Your VFR route crosses a MOA that may be active this afternoon. What is the best approach?
notes.back: B) You may cross, but check its status and contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories first
notes.choices:
A) Avoid it: VFR flight is prohibited in MOAs
B) You may cross, but check its status and contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories first
C) Cross at any altitude with no precautions
notes.choicesExplained: A: MOAs do not prohibit VFR flight. C ignores the need for extreme caution when military activity is under way.
notes.explanation: MOA status can change often, so real-time information is needed.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-4-5, “Military Operations Areas”
notes.evidence: Prior to entering an active MOA, pilots should contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories.

notes.front: Under section 91.137, what surface hazard can lead to a temporary flight restriction?
notes.back: An incident on the surface whose hazard low-flying aircraft would magnify, alter, spread or compound.
notes.explanation: Examples include toxic gas leaks and imminent volcano eruptions.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-3, “Temporary Flight Restrictions”
notes.evidence: Protect persons and property in the air or on the surface from an existing or imminent hazard associated with an incident on the surface

notes.front: Which temporary flight restriction purpose protects aircraft such as firefighting aircraft?
notes.back: A safe environment for disaster relief aircraft (section 91.137(a)(2)).
notes.explanation: Forest fires fought with aerial retardant are one situation named.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-3, “Temporary Flight Restrictions”
notes.evidence: Provide a safe environment for the operation of disaster relief aircraft

notes.front: Which temporary flight restriction purpose deals with crowds of sightseeing aircraft?
notes.back: Preventing unsafe congestion of sightseeing aircraft above an incident or event of high public interest.
notes.explanation: It is section 91.137(a)(3).
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-3, “Temporary Flight Restrictions”
notes.evidence: Prevent an unsafe congestion of sightseeing aircraft above an incident or event which may generate a high degree of public interest

notes.front: Which temporary flight restrictions protect the President, Vice President or other public figures?
notes.back: Those under section 91.141.
notes.explanation: Space agency operations have their own restrictions under section 91.143.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-3, “Temporary Flight Restrictions”
notes.evidence: Protect the President, Vice President, or other public figures

notes.front: Local news reports a large forest fire near your route, with aircraft dropping retardant. What should you do?
notes.back: A) Check NOTAMs during planning and route clear of the restriction
notes.choices:
A) Check NOTAMs during planning and route clear of the restriction
B) Fly over it to get a look, staying above 1,000 feet
C) Enter it if you keep a listening watch
notes.choicesExplained: B: sightseeing congestion is exactly what these restrictions prevent. C: a listening watch gives no permission to enter.
notes.explanation: Pilots must comply with the restriction rules and should check NOTAMs during flight planning.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-3, “Temporary Flight Restrictions”
notes.evidence: Pilots are responsible to comply with 14 CFR sections 91.137, 91.138, 91.141 and 91.143 when conducting flight in an area where a temporary flight restrictions area is in effect, and should check appropriate NOTAMs during flight planning.

notes.front: What does a four-digit military training route number (such as `VR1207`) tell you?
notes.back: The route has no segment above 1,500 feet AGL.
notes.explanation: Routes with any segment above 1,500 feet AGL use three digits.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-2, “Military Training Routes”
notes.evidence: MTRs with no segment above 1,500 feet AGL must be identified by four number characters

notes.front: How do IR and VR military training routes differ?
notes.back: IR routes are flown under IFR whatever the weather; VR routes under VFR, with at least 5 miles visibility and a 3,000-foot ceiling.
notes.explanation: Both are for low-altitude, high-speed training, generally at over 250 knots below 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 3-5-2, “Military Training Routes”
notes.evidence: Operations on these routes are conducted in accordance with VFR except flight visibility must be 5 miles or more; and flights must not be conducted below a ceiling of less than 3,000 feet AGL.

notes.front: To fly VFR within 60 NM of Washington, D.C., what must a pilot in command have completed?
notes.back: The FAA’s Special Awareness Training, holding its certificate of completion.
notes.explanation: The free training covers procedures for the Washington area and special use airspace in general.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.161, “Special awareness training required for pilots flying under visual flight rules within a 60-nautical mile radius of the Washington, DC VOR/DME”
notes.evidence: unless that pilot has completed Special Awareness Training and holds a certificate of training completion

notes.front: Operating into or across the contiguous ADIZ, what transponder setting is required?
notes.back: On, squawking a discrete code assigned by ATC or Flight Service, with altitude; code 1200 is not authorised.
notes.explanation: The aim is early identification of every aircraft near national boundaries.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-4, “ADIZ Requirements”
notes.evidence: The transponder must be turned on and squawking a discrete beacon code assigned by ATC or issued by FSS and displaying the aircraft altitude. Use of beacon code 1200 is not authorized.

notes.front: What flight plan does the ADIZ require?
notes.back: An IFR or defense VFR flight plan with the time and point of ADIZ penetration, filed, activated and closed.
notes.explanation: A VFR flight plan filed in flight makes an aircraft subject to interception on entering an ADIZ.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-4, “ADIZ Requirements”
notes.evidence: Pilots must file an Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) flight plan or file a Defense Visual Flight Rules (DVFR) flight plan containing the time and point of ADIZ penetration

notes.front: May you fly aerobatics over a congested area of a city, town or settlement?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Section 91.303 bans aerobatics there outright.
notes.evidence: No person may operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight— (a) Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement;

notes.front: Over what gathering of people does section 91.303 forbid aerobatic flight, wherever it is?
notes.back: An open-air assembly of persons.
notes.explanation: It applies even outside a congested area.
notes.evidence: Over an open air assembly of persons;

notes.front: Within the lateral boundaries of which airspace surface areas is aerobatic flight banned?
notes.back: The surface areas of Class B, C, D or E designated for an airport.
notes.explanation: The ban follows the lateral boundaries, not just the airport itself.
notes.evidence: Within the lateral boundaries of the surface areas of Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E airspace designated for an airport;

notes.front: Within how far of the centre line of a Federal airway is aerobatic flight banned?
notes.back: 4 nautical miles.
notes.explanation: Federal airways are Class E routes used by en route traffic.
notes.evidence: Within 4 nautical miles of the center line of any Federal airway;

notes.front: Below what height above the surface is aerobatic flight banned?
notes.back: 1,500 feet.
notes.explanation: It is the only height limit among the section 91.303 restrictions.
notes.evidence: Below an altitude of 1,500 feet above the surface;

notes.front: Below what flight visibility is aerobatic flight banned?
notes.back: Less than 3 statute miles.
notes.explanation: It is the only weather limit in section 91.303.
notes.evidence: When flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles.

notes.front: You plan loops at 3,000 feet above open farmland, 2 NM from the centre line of a Federal airway, with 10 miles visibility. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B) No: you are too close to a Federal airway
notes.choices:
A) Yes: every condition in section 91.303 is met
B) No: you are too close to a Federal airway
C) No: you are too low
notes.choicesExplained: A misses the 4 NM airway limit. C: 3,000 feet is above the 1,500-foot minimum.
notes.explanation: Aerobatics are banned within 4 NM of a Federal airway’s centre line.
notes.evidence: Within 4 nautical miles of the center line of any Federal airway;

notes.front: Carrying a passenger who is not a crewmember, what manoeuvre limits apply unless everyone wears an approved parachute?
notes.back: No intentional bank over 60° or nose-up or nose-down attitude over 30°.
notes.explanation: The limits are measured relative to the horizon.
notes.evidence: A bank of 60 degrees relative to the horizon; or (2) A nose-up or nose-down attitude of 30 degrees relative to the horizon.

notes.front: Flying a friend for fun, you want to show a 70° bank turn. Neither of you wears a parachute. Is it allowed?
notes.back: B) No: without parachutes for everyone, bank may not exceed 60°
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the friend is strapped in
B) No: without parachutes for everyone, bank may not exceed 60°
C) Yes, because steep turns are normal flight
notes.choicesExplained: A: seat belts do not replace parachutes under this rule. C: the rule covers any intentional manoeuvre over 60° of bank.
notes.explanation: The exceptions are only for flight tests and required training with an instructor.
notes.evidence: A bank of 60 degrees relative to the horizon

notes.front: Above 12,500 feet up to and including 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude, when must the required crew use oxygen?
notes.back: For any part of the flight at those altitudes lasting more than 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: Only the required minimum flight crew is covered at these altitudes.
notes.evidence: At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet (MSL) up to and including 14,000 feet (MSL) unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration

notes.front: Above 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude, when must the required crew use oxygen?
notes.back: During the entire flight time at those altitudes.
notes.explanation: The 30-minute allowance ends at 14,000 feet.
notes.evidence: At cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 feet (MSL) unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes

notes.front: Above 15,000 feet cabin pressure altitude, what must each occupant be given?
notes.back: Supplemental oxygen (they must be provided with it).
notes.explanation: Passengers must be provided with it, not required to use it.
notes.evidence: At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet (MSL) unless each occupant of the aircraft is provided with supplemental oxygen.

notes.front: You will cruise at 13,500 feet cabin altitude for 45 minutes in an unpressurised aeroplane. What does section 91.211 require?
notes.back: B) The required crew must use oxygen for the time beyond 30 minutes at those altitudes
notes.choices:
A) No oxygen is needed below 14,000 feet
B) The required crew must use oxygen for the time beyond 30 minutes at those altitudes
C) Every passenger must use oxygen
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the 12,500-foot rule. C: passengers must only be provided with oxygen above 15,000 feet.
notes.explanation: Between 12,500 and 14,000 feet the crew need oxygen for the part of the flight over 30 minutes.
notes.evidence: for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration

notes.front: You plan to cross mountains at 15,500 feet cabin altitude with two passengers. What does section 91.211 require?
notes.back: B) The crew must use oxygen throughout, and each passenger must be provided with it
notes.choices:
A) Only the pilot needs oxygen
B) The crew must use oxygen throughout, and each passenger must be provided with it
C) Nobody needs oxygen for a short flight
notes.choicesExplained: A forgets the passengers above 15,000 feet. C: above 14,000 feet there is no time allowance at all.
notes.explanation: Above 14,000 feet the crew use it all the time; above 15,000 feet every occupant must be provided with it.
notes.evidence: At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet (MSL) unless each occupant of the aircraft is provided with supplemental oxygen.

notes.front: May the pilot in command allow an object to be dropped from the aircraft in flight?
notes.back: Not if it creates a hazard; it is allowed if reasonable precautions avoid injury or damage.
notes.explanation: The rule targets the hazard, not dropping as such.
notes.evidence: this section does not prohibit the dropping of any object if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property

notes.front: A night VFR flight to your first planned stop takes 1 hour at normal cruise, allowing for wind. What is the minimum flight time your fuel must allow?
notes.back: B) 1 hour 45 minutes
notes.choices:
A) 1 hour 30 minutes
B) 1 hour 45 minutes
C) 2 hours 15 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: A uses the day reserve. C adds a reserve for a return trip the rule does not require.
notes.explanation: The reserve is counted from the first point of intended landing: here 1 hour plus 45 minutes.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.151, “Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions”
notes.evidence: At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

notes.front: If intercepted, what transponder code should you select unless ATC instructs otherwise?
notes.explanation: It is one of the actions an intercepted aircraft must take without delay.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-13, “Interception Procedures”
notes.evidence: If transponder equipped, select Mode 3/A Code 7700 unless otherwise instructed by air traffic control.

notes.front: If intercepted, on what very high frequency guard channel should you try to call the interceptor or ATC?
notes.back: 121.5 MHz, giving your identity, position and the nature of the flight.
notes.explanation: The other guard frequency listed is 243.0 MHz.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-13, “Interception Procedures”
notes.evidence: making a general call on guard frequencies (121.5 or 243.0 MHz), giving the identity, position, and nature of the flight

notes.front: If ATC’s instructions conflict with the intercepting aircraft’s, what must an intercepted pilot do?
notes.back: Seek immediate clarification, and keep complying with the interceptor until positively released.
notes.explanation: The interceptor’s signals and instructions take effect until it releases you.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-13, “Interception Procedures”
notes.evidence: The crew of the intercepted aircraft must continue to comply with interceptor aircraft signals and instructions until positively released.

notes.front: By day, an interceptor rocks its wings from slightly above, ahead and to your left, then turns slowly. What does it mean?
notes.back: “You have been intercepted. Follow me.”
notes.explanation: The aeroplane replies by rocking its wings and following.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-14, “Interception Signals”
notes.evidence: DAY-Rocking wings from a position slightly above and ahead of, and normally to the left of, the intercepted aircraft

notes.front: What does an interceptor’s abrupt climbing break-away turn of 90° or more mean?
notes.back: “You may proceed.”
notes.explanation: The aeroplane acknowledges by rocking its wings.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-14, “Interception Signals”
notes.evidence: An abrupt break-away maneuver from the intercepted aircraft consisting of a climbing turn of 90 degrees or more without crossing the line of flight of the intercepted aircraft.

notes.front: A military aircraft pulls alongside, rocks its wings and starts a slow turn to the left. What do you do?
notes.back: B) Follow the interceptor’s signals, squawk 7700 and call on 121.5 MHz
notes.choices:
A) Ignore it and continue your planned route
B) Follow the interceptor’s signals, squawk 7700 and call on 121.5 MHz
C) Turn away sharply to keep clear of it
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the requirement to follow the interceptor’s instructions without delay.
notes.explanation: Rocking wings then a slow turn means “you have been intercepted, follow me”.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-6-13, “Interception Procedures”
notes.evidence: Adhere to instructions relayed through the use of visual devices, visual signals, and radio communications from the intercepting aircraft.
